title: Feature Engineering and Model Evaluation
subtitle: Prepare real, messy data for machine learning, evaluate models reliably with cross-validation, tune them honestly, and wrap it all in leak-proof scikit-learn pipelines.
outcomes: Apply and compare scaling and normalisation techniques, and tame skewed features and outliers
Impute missing values while keeping the information that missingness carries
Encode categorical variables appropriately, including high-cardinality features with leak-free target encoding
Implement k-fold, stratified, group and time-series cross-validation for robust evaluation
Optimise hyperparameters with grid, randomised and halving searches, and evaluate tuning with nested cross-validation
Construct scikit-learn pipelines that prevent data leakage, from raw columns to a saved model
prerequisites: Classical Classification and Clustering (or Machine Learning Foundations with Python): train/test splits, scikit-learn models and cross_val_score. Comfortable pandas. Install Python 3 with pandas, scikit-learn (1.3 or later for TargetEncoder; the outputs shown come from 1.9) and JupyterLab; SciPy and joblib come with scikit-learn. Every dataset comes with the labs.
description:
Models are only as good as the data they're given and the way they're judged. This course covers both halves, in scikit-learn. On the data side you scale features and learn when it matters, tame skewed values and outliers, fill in missing values while keeping the signal that missingness itself carries, and turn categories into numbers: one-hot and ordinal encoding, grouping rare levels, target encoding done without leaking the answer, and features from dates, text and interactions. On the evaluation side you use k-fold, stratified, group and time-series cross-validation, read several metrics and training scores at once, tune hyperparameters with grid, randomised and halving searches, and measure the tuning itself with nested cross-validation.

Everything comes together in pipelines: ColumnTransformer for mixed columns, custom steps, tuning preprocessing and model together, and saving the result as one object, with experiments that show how leakage inflates scores when a step is fitted in the wrong place. The labs work on a made-up club's season-ticket renewals, where every technique makes a measurable difference, and every lesson has a JupyterLab walkthrough with real outputs. The capstone is a robust, tuned pipeline for a new, messy dataset, evaluated honestly.

modules.title: Data Scaling & Preprocessing
modules.summary: Put numeric features on comparable scales, tame skew and outliers, and fill in missing values in ways that keep the information missingness carries, with every step fitted on training data only.

lessons.title: Why scale, and which scaler
objectives: Explain which models need scaled features, and why
Choose between StandardScaler, MinMaxScaler and RobustScaler
key_points: Scaling stops features with large ranges from dominating. Distance-based models (k-NN, k-means, SVMs), models trained by gradient descent and regularised linear models all depend on the features' scales; tree-based models don't, because each split compares one feature with a threshold.

StandardScaler removes the mean and scales to unit variance, z = (x − mean) / standard deviation. It suits roughly symmetric features, but one extreme value inflates the standard deviation and squeezes the other values together.
MinMaxScaler maps each feature to a range, [0, 1] by default. An outlier sets the end of the range, so the rest bunch up: with the values 1, 2, 3, 4 and 100, the first four land between 0 and 0.03.

RobustScaler subtracts the median and divides by the interquartile range, so outliers barely affect how the other values are scaled; MaxAbsScaler divides by the largest absolute value and keeps sparse data sparse.
Fit a scaler on the training data only and reuse its learned statistics (mean_ and scale_) on validation and test data; fitting it on all the data leaks information from the test set.
On the season-ticket data in the lab, k-NN's cross-validated ROC AUC rises from 0.517 unscaled to about 0.60 with any of the three scalers: scaling at all matters far more than which scaler.

steps.do: Scale five values, one of them an outlier, three ways.
steps.code:
import numpy as np
from sklearn.preprocessing import MinMaxScaler, RobustScaler, StandardScaler

x = np.array([[1.0], [2.0], [3.0], [4.0], [100.0]])
for scaler in (StandardScaler(), MinMaxScaler(), RobustScaler()):
    print(f"{type(scaler).__name__:<15}", scaler.fit_transform(x).ravel().round(2))
steps.see: StandardScaler squeezes the first four between -0.54 and -0.46, MinMaxScaler between 0 and 0.03; RobustScaler spreads them from -1 to 0.5 and leaves the outlier at 48.5.

lessons.title: Skewed features and outliers
objectives: Reduce right skew with log, power and quantile transforms
Handle outliers with limits learned from the training data
key_points: Many real features are right-skewed, with a long tail of large values, such as incomes, distances, counts and prices; skew lets a few large values dominate linear models and squeezes the rest together after scaling.
np.log1p(x), the logarithm of 1 + x, compresses large values and copes with zeros: on a log-normal sample it cuts the skewness from 3.87 to −0.07.

PowerTransformer learns a Yeo-Johnson transform (Box-Cox needs strictly positive values) that makes a feature as close to normal as it can, then standardises it; QuantileTransformer maps values through their ranks to a uniform or normal distribution, which also tames outliers.

Decide what an outlier is before acting: a data error should be fixed or removed, but a real extreme, such as a member who moved 300 km away, carries information; clipping (winsorising) caps it at a quantile learned from the training data.
FunctionTransformer(np.log1p) puts a fixed transform inside a pipeline, while fitted transformers such as PowerTransformer learn their parameters from the training folds only.

steps.do: Measure the skewness of a log-normal sample before and after log1p.
steps.code:
import numpy as np
from scipy.stats import skew

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
income = np.exp(rng.normal(10, 1, 1000))
print(round(skew(income), 2), round(skew(np.log1p(income)), 2))
steps.see: 3.87 before, -0.07 after.

steps.do: Try a power and a quantile transform on the same column.
steps.code:
from sklearn.preprocessing import PowerTransformer, QuantileTransformer

col = income.reshape(-1, 1)
for t in (PowerTransformer(), QuantileTransformer(output_distribution="normal", n_quantiles=200, random_state=0)):
    print(type(t).__name__, round(skew(t.fit_transform(col).ravel()), 2))
steps.see: Skewness 0.0 and -0.01: both make the column close to symmetric.

lessons.title: Missing values: imputation and indicators
objectives: Fill missing values with SimpleImputer, KNNImputer or IterativeImputer
Keep the information that missingness itself carries
key_points: Values can be missing completely at random, at random given the other features, or for reasons tied to the missing value itself; only in the first case does the fact that a value is missing carry no information.

Dropping incomplete rows wastes data and can bias it: on the season-ticket data it keeps 82.4% of members and raises the renewal rate from 0.712 to 0.754, because members with a missing match count renew far less often (0.295).

Imputation handles missing data: SimpleImputer fills each column with its mean, median, most frequent value or a constant, learned in fit. The median resists outliers, and most_frequent works for categories too.

add_indicator=True adds a 0/1 column for each feature that had gaps, so the model can learn from missingness itself: on the season-ticket data it lifts logistic regression's ROC AUC from 0.642 to 0.710.

KNNImputer fills a gap from the most similar rows, and IterativeImputer models each feature from the others (after from sklearn.experimental import enable_iterative_imputer); they can be more accurate but are slower, and need scaled features.
HistGradientBoosting models accept NaN directly, learning at each split which side the missing values should go.

modules.title: Categorical Encoding
modules.summary: Turn categories and text into numbers: one-hot encoding for unordered categories, ordinal encoding for ordered ones, grouping or target encoding for many categories, and simple features from dates, text and interactions.

lessons.title: One-hot and ordinal encoding
objectives: Choose between one-hot and ordinal encoding
Handle unknown and rare categories with OneHotEncoder
key_points: Models require numerical input, so categories must become numbers, and how matters: the codes 0, 1 and 2 for unordered categories invent an order and spacing that linear and distance-based models will use.

One-hot encoding creates one binary column per category. handle_unknown='ignore' encodes a category never seen in training as all zeros instead of raising an error, and drop='if_binary' keeps a single column for a yes/no feature.

Ordinal encoding is for ordered categories, such as bronze < silver < gold. Give the order with OrdinalEncoder(categories=[['bronze', 'silver', 'gold']]), because by default it sorts alphabetically: bronze 0, gold 1, silver 2.

Rare categories get their own one-hot column but almost no data: min_frequency or max_categories groups them into one infrequent column (named infrequent_sklearn), and handle_unknown='infrequent_if_exist' sends new categories there too.
Tree ensembles can work with ordinal codes even for unordered categories, and HistGradientBoosting supports categorical features natively; linear models and k-NN need one-hot encoding.

lessons.title: High-cardinality features and target encoding
objectives: Explain target encoding and its leakage risk
Use TargetEncoder's cross fitting and smoothing
key_points: A feature with many categories, such as a postcode or a seat block, one-hot encodes into many sparse columns. Alternatives are grouping rare levels, count (frequency) encoding, hashing, or target encoding.

Target encoding uses the target variable: it replaces each category with the mean target for that category, shrunk towards the overall mean when the category is rare (smoothing), giving one informative column.

Computed on all the data before splitting, it leaks the answer, because each row's own label is inside its encoding: on a column of 150 random seat blocks with no real signal, that naive encoding scores a ROC AUC of 0.877; done properly, 0.530.

scikit-learn's TargetEncoder (version 1.3 and later) prevents this with cross fitting: fit_transform encodes each fold's rows with means learned on the other folds, while transform, used on new data, applies encodings learned on all the training data. Keep it inside the pipeline.

smooth='auto' chooses the shrinkage from the data. For repeatable results pass cv a splitter with a random_state, as in cv=StratifiedKFold(5, shuffle=True, random_state=0) (before version 1.9, set TargetEncoder's own random_state instead).

steps.do: Target-encode three categories with smoothing.
steps.code:
import numpy as np
from sklearn.model_selection import KFold
from sklearn.preprocessing import TargetEncoder

X = np.array([["a"]] * 6 + [["b"]] * 4 + [["c"]] * 2)
y = np.array([1, 1, 1, 0, 1, 1, 0, 0, 1, 0, 1, 0])
enc = TargetEncoder(smooth=2.0, cv=KFold(n_splits=3, shuffle=True, random_state=0))
cross_fitted = enc.fit_transform(X, y).ravel()
print(enc.categories_[0], np.round(enc.encodings_[0], 3), round(enc.target_mean_, 3))
steps.see: Encodings [0.771 0.361 0.542] around an overall mean of 0.583: c, with only 2 rows, stays close to the mean.

lessons.title: Dates, text and interactions
objectives: Turn dates and cyclical values into numeric features
Create interaction and text features
key_points: Dates become features through their parts, such as the month, the day of the week and the day of the year (pandas' .dt accessors), or through durations, such as days since the last purchase.

Cyclical features, such as months or hours, wrap round, so encode them as the sine and cosine of an angle: December and January are then as close as June and July (0.518 apart), and January and July the furthest apart (2.0).
Short text columns can become bag-of-words counts with CountVectorizer or TfidfVectorizer, applied to that column inside a ColumnTransformer.

Interactions, such as products and ratios of features, let linear models capture effects that depend on two features together; PolynomialFeatures(interaction_only=True) creates every pairwise product.
Every created feature must be computable at prediction time from information available then; a feature built from the future, or from the label, leaks.

modules.title: Cross-Validation Techniques
modules.summary: Estimate performance reliably without overfitting to a single test split: k-fold and stratified k-fold, groups and time order, repeated runs, several metrics at once, and what all those fits cost.

lessons.title: k-fold and stratified k-fold
objectives: Explain how k-fold cross-validation works and when to stratify
Choose k, and read the spread of the fold scores
key_points: K-fold splits the data into k subsets, the folds; each fold is the test set once while the model trains on the other k − 1, so every row is tested exactly once, and the k scores are averaged.
Stratified k-fold maintains class proportions in every fold: with 10 positives in 100 rows, KFold without shuffling can put all 10 in the last fold, while StratifiedKFold puts 2 in each.
KFold and StratifiedKFold don't shuffle by default, so data sorted by label or by time gives nonsense folds; pass shuffle=True with a random_state, unless the order itself matters, as with time.
An integer cv, such as cv=5, means StratifiedKFold(5) without shuffling for classifiers and KFold(5) for regressors.
Averaging over folds reduces the variance of the performance estimate compared with one split, and the spread of the fold scores shows how much the result depends on which rows were held out.
It is computationally more expensive, k fits instead of one; 5 or 10 folds are the usual choice, with more folds giving each model more training data but taking longer.

lessons.title: Groups, time and repeated cross-validation
objectives: Keep related rows together with group k-fold
Respect time order with TimeSeriesSplit
Get steadier estimates with repeated cross-validation
key_points: When several rows come from one entity, such as the sessions of one player or the visits of one patient, random folds put the same entity in training and test, and the model scores well just by recognising it. GroupKFold keeps each group in a single fold.
In the lab's made-up sessions data, where the label has nothing to do with the features, 1-nearest-neighbour scores 0.955 accuracy with shuffled KFold and 0.487, about chance, with GroupKFold.

For time-ordered data, TimeSeriesSplit trains on the past and tests on the period after it, with a growing training window; gap leaves rows out between training and test, and test_size fixes each test window.
RepeatedStratifiedKFold reruns stratified k-fold with different shuffles, such as 5 folds × 10 repeats = 50 scores, for a steadier mean and a clearer view of the spread.
Leave-one-out uses n folds of one row each: nearly all the data trains each model, but it costs n fits and its estimate can vary a lot.

lessons.title: Metrics, training scores and learning curves
objectives: Score cross-validation with several metrics at once
Diagnose overfitting with training scores and learning curves
key_points: scoring chooses the metric, such as 'roc_auc', 'f1', 'balanced_accuracy' or 'neg_log_loss'. Error metrics are negated, as in 'neg_mean_absolute_error', so that higher is always better.
cross_validate returns a dictionary with fit times, score times and the test scores of several metrics at once, plus the training scores with return_train_score=True.

A large gap between training and test scores signals overfitting: an unpruned tree scores a training ROC AUC of 1.000 and a test ROC AUC of 0.555 on the season-ticket data, where logistic regression scores 0.730 and 0.711.
learning_curve trains on growing subsets: a test score still rising at the full size means more data would help; training and test scores meeting at a low level mean the model is too simple.
Compare models on the same folds by passing the same cv object, and look at the spread as well as the mean: differences smaller than the fold-to-fold spread may be noise.

modules.summary: Search systematically for the best model settings: exhaustive grid search, randomised search over distributions, successive halving, and nested cross-validation to measure the whole tuning process honestly.

lessons.title: Hyperparameters and grid search
objectives: Tell hyperparameters from learned parameters
Run GridSearchCV and read its results
key_points: Hyperparameters are set before training, in the constructor, such as C, max_depth or n_neighbors; parameters such as coef_ are learned by fit. get_params() lists the hyperparameters, and pipeline steps prefix their names, as in svc__C.

GridSearchCV tries all combinations of the values given and scores each by cross-validation: 3 values of C and 3 of gamma with 5 folds mean 45 fits. With refit=True, the default, it then refits the best combination on all the data.
best_params_, best_score_ and best_estimator_ give the winner, and cv_results_ holds every candidate's mean and standard deviation, worth reading because near-ties are common.
Space values of C, gamma, alpha or learning rates on a log scale, such as 0.01, 0.1, 1 and 10, and widen the grid when the best value sits on its edge.
A grid grows multiplicatively with every hyperparameter, so it suits a few hyperparameters with a few values each; set scoring to the metric that matters, and n_jobs=-1 to use every core.

lessons.title: Nested cross-validation
objectives: Explain why best_score_ is optimistic
Evaluate a tuning process with nested cross-validation
key_points: best_score_ is biased upwards: the same folds both choose the hyperparameters and score them, so with many candidates some win partly by luck.

Nested cross-validation evaluates the tuning process: an outer loop splits the data, an inner GridSearchCV tunes on each outer training set, and the outer test folds, never seen by the tuning, give the estimate: cross_val_score(GridSearchCV(...), X, y, cv=outer).
On random data with no signal, a 20-candidate SVM grid reports a best_score_ of 0.525 while nested cross-validation gives 0.475; on the season-ticket data the grid's 0.694 becomes 0.659 nested.
Nested cross-validation estimates how well the whole procedure does, not one set of hyperparameters; the final model is then tuned with the same procedure on all the training data.
It is expensive, outer folds × inner folds × candidates fits (5 × 5 × 20 = 500 here), so use it to report performance and compare procedures rather than at every step.

modules.title: scikit-learn Pipelines
modules.summary: Chain preprocessing and modelling so that every step runs in the right order on the right data: ColumnTransformer for mixed columns, leak-proof cross-validation, custom steps, tuning preprocessing and model together, and saving the whole workflow as one object.

lessons.title: Pipelines and ColumnTransformer for mixed data
objectives: Prepare numeric and categorical columns differently in one ColumnTransformer
Name and reach the parameters of nested steps
key_points: Pipelines encapsulate workflows: a Pipeline chains transformers and a final model, so fit runs every step in order on the training data, and predict applies the same fitted steps to new data.

ColumnTransformer sends different columns to different transformers, by name or with make_column_selector(dtype_include='number'); remainder='drop', the default, drops the other columns, and remainder='passthrough' keeps them.

set_output(transform='pandas') makes the steps return DataFrames with feature names, such as num__age and cat__tier_gold, and get_feature_names_out() lists them: the easiest way to check what the model sees.
Step names build parameter paths: make_pipeline names steps after their classes in lower case, so the imputer inside a ColumnTransformer's num step is columntransformer__num__simpleimputer__strategy.
A pipeline simplifies deployment: one object to fit, cross-validate, tune, save and load, with no preprocessing code to repeat at prediction time.

    ("cat", OneHotEncoder(sparse_output=False), ["tier"]),

lessons.title: Leakage, and how pipelines prevent it
objectives: Recognise data leakage during cross-validation
Explain why preprocessing must be fitted inside each training fold
key_points: Data leakage is information from outside the training data, often from the test folds or the label itself, reaching the model during training, which makes scores look better than the model will do on new data.

Any step that learns from data, such as scaling, imputing, encoding, selecting features or resampling, leaks if it is fitted before the split. Pipelines prevent data leakage during CV: cross-validation refits every step on each training fold.

The size of a leak depends on how much the step learns: scaling the breast cancer data before cross-validation changes nothing measurable (0.9789 both ways), but choosing 20 of 5,000 random features on all 100 rows lifts cross-validated accuracy on a random label to 0.830, against 0.510 inside the pipeline.

Target leakage comes from features that wouldn't exist at prediction time, such as a 'renewal letter sent' column filled in after the outcome: one such column drives a cross-validated ROC AUC to 0.9995. Scores that look too good usually are.
Other leaks: duplicate rows split across folds, rows of one entity in both training and test (use groups), and future information in time series (use TimeSeriesSplit).

lessons.title: Custom steps, tuning everything together, and saving
objectives: Write a custom transformer that learns in fit
Tune preprocessing choices and models together
Save and reload a fitted pipeline safely
key_points: FunctionTransformer wraps a fixed function, such as np.log1p, as a step; a custom transformer class with fit and transform, inheriting from BaseEstimator and TransformerMixin, handles steps that learn from data, such as clipping limits.

Learn state only in fit, from the data passed to it, and store it in attributes ending in an underscore; let __init__ only store hyperparameters, so that clone and get_params work and GridSearchCV can copy the step.

OneToOneFeatureMixin gives a custom transformer get_feature_names_out for one output column per input column, so it works with set_output(transform='pandas'); record feature_names_in_ in fit when the input has column names.

A pipeline can tune preprocessing and model together: a grid can change a step's settings (prep__num__simpleimputer__strategy), replace a step ('scale': [StandardScaler(), RobustScaler()]) or skip it ('passthrough'), and a list of grids can compare model families.
joblib.dump saves a fitted pipeline and joblib.load restores it; load files only from sources you trust, because loading can run code, and load with the scikit-learn version that saved it.

steps.do: Write a transformer that learns each column's median in fit, and check that clone can copy it.
steps.code:
import numpy as np
from sklearn.base import BaseEstimator, OneToOneFeatureMixin, TransformerMixin, clone


class CentreOnMedian(OneToOneFeatureMixin, TransformerMixin, BaseEstimator):
    """Subtract each column's training median."""

    def fit(self, X, y=None):
        self.median_ = np.median(np.asarray(X, dtype=float), axis=0)
        self.n_features_in_ = np.asarray(X).shape[1]
        return self

    def transform(self, X):
        return np.asarray(X, dtype=float) - self.median_


step = CentreOnMedian().fit([[1.0], [2.0], [10.0]])
print(step.median_, step.transform([[5.0]]), clone(step).get_params())
steps.see: [2.] [[3.]] {}: the median learned in fit, applied in transform; no hyperparameters to copy.

from sklearn.datasets import load_breast_cancer
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.model_selection import GridSearchCV, StratifiedKFold
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import RobustScaler, StandardScaler

grid = [{"scale": [StandardScaler(), RobustScaler()], "model__C": [0.1, 1]},

print(search.best_params_, round(search.best_score_, 4))
